sections.html: The common length of C. harcourtbutleri is between 8 and 15 cm; the largest specimen known so far was 18.5 cm long (all measurements are standard length, without the caudal fin). The photographed specimens have a standard length of about 11 cm (male) and 9 cm (female) and are sexually ripe.

Channa harcourtbutleri occurs in Burma at higher elevations, where it can become fairly cool. It is therefore better not to keep this species at high, tropical temperatures the whole year round. Regarding water, the fish is very undemanding, but very soft and acidic water should be avoided.
No detailed breeding report is known, but it is very likely that there are no major differences from C. gachua, which is a biparental mouthbrooding species.

This only very rarely offered snakehead was obtained from Burma. The species is a very close relative of Channa gachua and was considered a mere synonym of C. gachua for a very long time. Ng, Ng & Britz showed in 1999 that C. harcourtbutleri is a valid species. However, both species look very similar. C. harcourtbutleri has a narrower head and (this is mood-dependent and not always visible) a dark marbled throat (uniform in C. gachua). Moreover, juveniles of C. harcourtbutleri lack the ocellus in the dorsal fin that is typical for juveniles of C. gachua. There are further minor differences in the pattern, but due to the extreme mood-dependent change of coloration in snakeheads these differences are of no use for identification. It is also more than likely that many populations and described species currently placed in C. gachua will prove to be species in their own right, so it is very difficult to speak of a typical pattern and coloration in C. gachua.
